What the official sources say

  • A valuation complaint for the current tax year is filed with the county auditor on or before March 31 of the ensuing tax year or the closing date of first-half collection, whichever is later. (ORC 5715.19(A)(1) (eff. Mar. 20, 2026); source)
  • For homestead reduction, 'sixty-five years of age or older' means a person who attained age 64 before Jan 1 of the application year; permanently and totally disabled defined by impairment on Jan 1 of application year or agency certification. (ORC 323.151(B), (D); source)
  • The ORC 319.302 partial exemption (non-business-credit rollback) as amended (latest legislation HB 186, 136th GA; version eff. Mar. 20, 2026) provides 10% for farming property and, for residential property, 7.5% for the first tax year the amendment applies, with cumulative 2.5-point reductions in each of the following two years and 0% thereafter. The older flat '2.5% rollback' for owner-occupied residential should NOT be stated as current. (ORC 319.302(B) (excerpt only; full text and applicability dates not seen); source)

(ORC 5721.25 (eff. Apr. 7, 2009); excerpt partial; source)
  • 'Tax certificate' under 5721.30 is a document (physical, book-entry or electronic) at the treasurer's discretion and is distinct from the delinquent land tax certificate under 5721.13; 'certificate parcel' means the delinquent land described in a tax certificate. (ORC 5721.30(A)-(B) (eff. Nov. 2, 2018); source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in Ohio?

Ohio estate tax FAQ

Does Ohio have an estate tax?

The Department of Taxation says the estate tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2013.

Does Ohio charge an estate tax?

No. The Ohio Department of Taxation reports that House Bill 153 repealed the state estate tax for every estate with a date of death in 2013 or later. House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly then added a sunset for the older estates: nothing is owed on property first discovered after December 31, 2021, or on property found earlier but never disclosed or reported by that date.

So an Ohio family selling an inherited house does not file a state estate tax return before closing. The Department also says it has dropped the requirement for ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms before a decedent's assets move to another person, and it asked county auditors and banks to stop forwarding them.

Could the federal estate tax reach an Ohio estate?

Only a very large one. For deaths in 2026 the IRS lists $15,000,000 as the basic exclusion amount, raised by Public Law 119-21, which was signed July 4, 2025. A single house rarely comes near that line, so for most families the federal return does not set the timeline.

The IRS adds two points. An estate that does not have to file a federal return should skip Form 8971, and the estate of someone survived by a spouse may elect to pass unused exclusion to that spouse on a timely filed return.

Who signs the deed when an inherited Ohio house is sold?

Usually the executor or administrator, under the supervision of the probate court that serves the decedent's home county. Ohio's land-sale procedure for executors, administrators and guardians runs from R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43, and an executor whose will grants a power of sale may follow the will instead.

Smaller estates may not need full administration. Under R.C. 2113.03 the court can release an estate from administration at $35,000 in assets or under, or up to $100,000 when a surviving spouse takes everything. The order can direct delivery of personal property and transfer of real property, and the court may appoint a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers. A buyer who pays value in good faith gets the same protection from unsecured creditors that administration would give.

  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate fits a release or needs letters of authority.
  • Gather the death certificate, the will, and the vesting deed.
  • Order a title search early so liens surface before a buyer finds them.

What changes if the owner recorded a transfer on death affidavit?

Title may already sit with the named beneficiary. R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner sign a verified transfer on death designation affidavit and record it with the county recorder before death. At the owner's death, title vests in the beneficiaries the affidavit names.

The affidavit needs neither payment nor delivery to work, and the recorder charges the deed fee and indexes it under the owner's name. Heirs who suspect a parent signed one should ask the recorder to search that name. Knowingly false statements in the affidavit are falsification under R.C. 2921.13.

What tax do heirs face when they sell an inherited Ohio house?

The IRS measures gain from the heir's basis, which for inherited property generally equals the fair market value at the date of death. Estates that elected the alternate valuation date use that figure, and farm or business land can use special-use valuation. Publication 551 says an heir who received no Schedule A (Form 8971) from the executor can rely on the appraised date-of-death value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

That makes an early appraisal worth ordering. Keep it with the estate papers so the tax preparer can apply it to the final price.

Who handles each step of an inherited-house sale in Ohio
StepOfficeAuthority
Release from administration or land saleProbate courtR.C. 2113.03; R.C. 2127.01
Transfer on death affidavit searchCounty recorderR.C. 5302.22
County transfer tax paid at deed deliveryCounty auditorR.C. 322.02
Valuation complaintCounty auditor, then board of revisionR.C. 5715.19

Source: Ohio Revised Code sections shown.

On the transfer tax, R.C. 322.02 caps any county levy at thirty cents for each hundred dollars of value, charged to the seller named in the deed and paid at the auditor's office before recording. Ask the county auditor which rate the house falls under.

Can an heir challenge the county's value of the house?

An owner can. R.C. 5715.19 sends a valuation complaint to the county auditor, with a filing deadline of March 31 of the following tax year unless first-half collection closes later. The county board of revision decides it, and the statute limits repeat complaints on one parcel within the same interim period unless something changed, such as an arm's length sale, a casualty loss or a substantial improvement.

A date-of-death appraisal can back up a complaint when the county figure looks high. The auditor's office can say which tax year a new filing would cover.

What will a buyer and title company ask the estate to provide?

Expect requests for proof of who has authority to sign, because a title company will not insure a deed it cannot trace. For an estate in administration that means the executor's or administrator's letters of authority from the probate court. For a released estate it means a copy of the release order. For a house covered by a transfer on death affidavit, it means the recorded affidavit and a death certificate.

The title company also searches for mortgages, judgments and unpaid tax. Because Ohio land sales by fiduciaries follow the statute, a sale that skips the court steps can leave a buyer with a cloud on title. If the file is complicated, a probate attorney in the home county can confirm which documents the closing will need before you accept an offer.

What should an Ohio heir do first?

Begin with whatever decides who may sign, then turn to the house. The probate clerk is the first call.

  • Find the original will and file it with the probate court if no one has.
  • Keep the house insured and secured, and redirect the mail.
  • Ask the recorder whether a transfer on death affidavit exists.
  • Request the current tax bill from the county treasurer.
  • Order the date-of-death appraisal.

An estate that needs to move quickly sometimes sells to a buyer who purchases without repairs or showings. If that fits, compare offers on what the estate keeps after transfer tax, payoffs and costs, since those items apply whichever way the house sells.

More questions about Ohio Estate Tax

Does Ohio have an estate tax in 2026?

No. The Ohio Department of Taxation says the tax was repealed for estates with a 2013 or later date of death, and the House Bill 110 sunset ended collection on property first discovered after December 31, 2021.

Do I need a state tax release to transfer a parent's Ohio house?

No. The Department of Taxation says it no longer requires the ET 12, 13 or 14 release forms. Title and probate steps still apply, so ask the probate court clerk what the estate needs.

Is there a federal estate tax on a modest Ohio estate?

Not at that size. The IRS lists $15,000,000 as the federal basic exclusion amount for 2026 deaths and $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths, and estates under that amount are not required to file Form 706 for that reason.

Can a house pass without full probate in Ohio?

Sometimes. A recorded transfer on death affidavit vests title in the named beneficiary under R.C. 5302.22, and a probate court can release an estate with $35,000 or less in assets under R.C. 2113.03. The probate court can tell you which path fits.

Who pays the county transfer tax when an estate sells in Ohio?

The seller named in the deed. R.C. 322.02 puts the charge on the grantor, payable to the county auditor before the deed reaches the recorder, at a rate each county sets within the thirty-cent cap.

title: Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House
content:
Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Ohio
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale
  • Turn the Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling an Ohio House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • To begin an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) action, the party must give the adverse party notice to leave at least three days before filing, by certified mail, hand delivery, or leaving at the abode/premises, except as provided in (B) or (C). (ORC 1923.04(A) (eff. Oct. 18, 2007); source)
Selling in Ohio?
We buy Ohio houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How long does an Ohio eviction take from filing to move-out?

Ohio Legal Help says an eviction is a process that can take four to six weeks, so a tenant's belongings are not set out the next day. Once a landlord files, the court sends a summons and the hearing usually falls about two weeks later.

Cold weather does not pause the case. The same guide states that a tenant can be evicted in Ohio even in winter. For an owner who plans to sell, that four to six week stretch begins only after the written notice has run, so the calendar from notice to an empty house is longer than the court phase alone.

What are the steps in an Ohio eviction case?

Chapter 1923 of the Revised Code, the forcible entry and detainer chapter, sets the sequence. Each step below leads to the next, and a landlord who skips one risks a dismissal.

  • Written notice to leave, given at least three days before the case begins (R.C. 1923.04).
  • Complaint filed with the municipal or county court that covers the rental address.
  • Summons issued and served, at least seven days before trial (R.C. 1923.06).
  • Hearing before a judge unless a jury is demanded or the case is continued (R.C. 1923.09).
  • Judgment for restitution of the premises plus court costs.
  • Writ of execution requested and carried out by the sheriff, a police officer, a constable or a court bailiff (R.C. 1923.13 and 1923.14).
Ohio eviction stages and timing
StageTimingSource
Notice to leaveThree or more days before filingR.C. 1923.04
Service of summonsAt least seven days before the trial dateR.C. 1923.06(A)
Hearing on possessionNo sooner than the seventh day after service is completeR.C. 1923.06(H)
Answer to extra money claimsTwenty-eight days after service is completeR.C. 1923.06(H)
Officer carries out the writWithin ten days after receiving itR.C. 1923.14(A)

Source: Ohio Revised Code, Chapter 1923.

How is the summons served on an Ohio tenant?

The clerk always mails the summons and a copy of the complaint by ordinary mail, with a certificate of mailing. The plaintiff then picks a second method when filing: personal-type service by a sheriff, a court bailiff or an adult the court designates, or certified mail with return receipt.

The person serving process goes to the rental. If the tenant is there, the papers are handed over. If not, they are left with someone of suitable age and discretion at the address. If neither works, a copy is posted in a conspicuous place on the premises. That person must return the process to the clerk within five days and note which method was used.

Service counts as complete when the first two methods are used, or when ordinary mailing and posting have both happened. The summons itself carries a notice that a tenant depositing rent with the clerk must keep depositing it until the hearing, that a jury trial may be requested, and that free legal help may be available.

What happens at the hearing and what can the judgment include?

If no one asks for a jury or a continuance, a judge tries the case and can reach one of three results under R.C. 1923.09.

  • Complaint true: judgment for restitution of the premises to the landlord, with costs of suit.
  • Complaint true in part: restitution for that part only, with costs divided as the judge sees fit.
  • Complaint not true: judgment against the landlord for costs.

R.C. 1923.081 allows the same trial to include the landlord's claims for past due rent and other damages, unless the court continues those claims for good cause. A tenant's request to file an answer, a counterclaim or to take discovery counts as good cause, and the case then runs like other civil cases. Ohio Legal Help adds that a tenant who needs time to find a lawyer can ask for a continuance, and that agreements reached before the hearing should be in writing and told to the judge.

How does the writ of eviction work after judgment?

After a judgment of restitution, the landlord asks the court to issue a writ of execution. Ohio Legal Help says a red tag is posted on the door telling the tenant how long remains to leave, and that the period is generally five days. After that the landlord can ask the officer to set the tenant's things out.

R.C. 1923.14 says the officer must carry out the writ within ten days after receiving it by restoring the landlord to possession. A tenant who appeals and obtains a stay of execution after posting any required bond can pause the removal, and the judge then orders the officer to delay further proceedings.

How does an eviction affect the sale of a rented Ohio house?

A pending case does not stop an owner from signing a purchase contract, but the buyer cannot take possession until the tenant leaves voluntarily or the writ is carried out. Buyers who want the house vacant will often ask the seller to finish the court process first. Other buyers purchase the house with the tenant in place.

Ohio's self-help ban still applies while the sale is in progress. A landlord may not shut off utilities or lock the tenant out to speed things up (R.C. 5321.15), and a retaliatory possession action can be raised as a defense (R.C. 5321.02).

Manufactured home parks follow their own end steps. If an evicted resident leaves a home unoccupied for three days after judgment, the operator may give the titled owner written notice to remove it within fourteen days. A home worth more than three thousand dollars goes to a sheriff's sale within sixty days of the writ. A home worth three thousand dollars or less can have its title transferred to the plaintiff within thirty days, through the clerk of the common pleas title division.

Where can Ohio landlords and tenants get help with an eviction case?

Start with the clerk of the court named on the summons, who can explain local filing and hearing procedures but cannot give legal advice. Ohio Legal Help lists free legal aid by county, and Akron, Cleveland, Columbus and Toledo have Right to Counsel programs for some tenants with low income. Owners with several rentals often hire a landlord attorney, because a missed deadline can force them to restart the notice and filing sequence. Keep a file with the lease, the rent ledger, the notice, proof of delivery and every court paper, since the judge and the buyer will both ask for them.

More questions about Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How many days does a tenant have to leave after an Ohio eviction judgment?

Ohio Legal Help says the posted red tag generally allows five days. After that the landlord can ask the sheriff or bailiff to carry out the writ, which the officer must execute within ten days after receiving it.

Can a landlord evict a tenant in the winter in Ohio?

Yes. Ohio Legal Help states that evictions can happen in winter or very cold weather. The case follows the same notice, hearing and writ steps as in any other season.

What is the earliest an Ohio eviction hearing can be held?

No sooner than the seventh day after service of the summons is complete, under R.C. 1923.06(H). Service must be made at least seven days before the day set for trial.

Can a landlord collect back rent in the same Ohio case?

Often yes. R.C. 1923.081 allows the trial to include claims for past due rent and other damages, unless the court continues those claims for good cause such as a tenant's request to answer or take discovery.

Does an eviction filing stop a sale of the house?

No. An owner can still sell, but possession depends on the tenant leaving or the writ being carried out. A buyer who wants a vacant house usually asks the seller to complete the court process before closing.

An Ohio deed is recorded with the county recorder, and the conveyance fee can apply.

What the official sources say

  • A deed must be signed by the grantor and the signing acknowledged before a judge or clerk of a court of record, county auditor, county engineer, notary public, or mayor. (ORC 5301.01(A) (eff. Jan. 30, 2014); source)
  • Transfer on death designation affidavits are recorded by the county recorder in the same manner and for the same fee as deeds. (ORC 5302.22(E); source)
  • Deeds and instruments conveying land must be recorded with the county recorder where the premises lie; until recorded they are fraudulent as to a subsequent bona fide purchaser without knowledge. (ORC 5301.25(A); source)
  • Land installment contracts must be recorded within 20 days after signing by both parties and a copy delivered to the county auditor. (ORC 5313.02(C); source)
  • The mandatory county auditor real property transfer (conveyance) fee is $1 or 10 cents per $100 (or fraction) of value of real property transferred, whichever is greater, with listed exemptions (e.g., transfers to confirm/correct a deed, gifts between spouses or parent and child, pursuant to court order not resulting from a sale, no-consideration transfers, transfers to a revocable trust). (ORC 319.54(G)(3) (eff. Apr. 9, 2025); source)
  • The grantor (seller) pays the 319.54(G)(3) fee and any county real property transfer tax levied under ORC Chapter 322 at deed delivery, via statement of value filed with the county auditor. (ORC 319.202(D) (eff. Sept. 30, 2025); source)
  • A county may levy an additional (permissive) real property transfer tax not exceeding 30 cents per $100 of value; the tax is levied on and paid by the grantor to the county auditor before the deed is presented to the recorder. (ORC 322.02(A) (eff. Apr. 9, 2025); source)

title: Ohio Closing Costs: Conveyance Fee, Recording and What Sellers Pay
content:
Ohio Closing Costs: Conveyance Fee, Recording and What Sellers Pay

Cash Home Buyers in Ohio
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Ohio Closing Costs: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Ohio Closing Costs sale
  • Turn the Ohio Closing Costs offer down and you owe us nothing

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in Ohio?
We buy Ohio houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • County permissive rates by county.

What closing costs does an Ohio seller pay?

An Ohio seller's costs are driven by a few statutory charges plus whatever the purchase contract assigns. The statutory ones are the county auditor's conveyance fee, a possible county transfer tax, a small per-parcel transfer fee and, on paper filings, any recording charge the contract puts on the seller. The rest comes from the contract: payoff of your mortgage and prorations for taxes and similar items.

Ohio law is specific about only some of these. Everything in the table below comes from the Revised Code, so use it as a checklist of the charges the legislature wrote down, and then ask the title agent for the line items on your own closing statement.

Ohio charges set by statute that touch a home sale
ChargeRate as printedSection
Conveyance fee, paid to the county auditor$1 or ten cents per $100 or fraction, whichever is greater319.54(G)(3)
Optional county real property transfer taxUp to thirty cents per $100322.02(A)
Auditor's entry of a land transferFifty cents per transfer319.54(G)(2)
Recording the first two pages of an instrument$17 base plus $17 housing trust fund317.32(A)
Each added page$4 base plus $4 housing trust fund317.32(A)
Optional document preservation surchargeUp to $5 per instrument317.32(A)

Who pays the Ohio conveyance fee?

The grantor, which means the seller. Section 319.202 says the grantor pays the fee under 319.54(G)(3) and any transfer tax levied under Chapter 322 at the time the deed is delivered. Auditor first, recorder second, is the order of stops.

The fee is measured against "value", which the section defines in that section as the full consideration paid or to be paid, including the amount of any mortgage or vendor's lien. For a gift, value means the open-market price between a willing buyer and a willing seller. The law also bars anyone from willfully falsifying the stated value.

Do Ohio counties charge different conveyance rates?

Yes. State law fixes the floor, and commissioners may add a tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars under section 322.02. To adopt it, the board must hold two public hearings and publish notice, and the resolution is generally open to a referendum.

Two counties show how the printed figure is expressed. The Morrow County Auditor's page lists $4.00 per thousand for both real estate and manufactured homes. The Muskingum County Auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand too, calculated by multiplying the sale price by 0.004 and rounding to the nearest ten cents, along with a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee. Other counties publish different numbers, so open your own county auditor's real estate transfer page, or phone the office, before you estimate proceeds.

Which Ohio transfers skip the conveyance fee?

The exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3) matter most to families and estates. Among them:

  • A deed whose sole purpose is to confirm or correct one already recorded.
  • A gift between spouses, or between a parent and a child or that child's spouse.
  • A transfer among heirs at law or devisees of a common decedent when no money is paid.
  • A deed to the trustee of a trust whose maker reserved an unlimited power to revoke.
  • A transfer to or from a person where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and the deal is not a gift.
  • A transfer by court order, as long as it is not the result of a sale made under that order.
  • An interest worth $100 or less.

When a transfer is exempt, the statement of value need only give the reason for the exemption.

How much does recording cost in Ohio?

The recorder's charges come from section 317.32 and are the same set of base and housing trust fund amounts in every county. The statute counts the caption page and any partial page, measured at eight and one-half by fourteen inches, so a deed with exhibits costs more than a short one.

The statute also says fees are due when the instrument is presented, apart from electronic filings, which may be settled afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method. It does not say which party to a sale bears the deed's recording cost. Look at your purchase contract, or ask the title agent, to see who is assigned that line.

What happens to the tax bill when an Ohio house closes?

Ohio real estate taxes are billed in two installments, and the Revised Code's default due dates in section 323.12 are December 31 and June 20. Counties set their own closing dates, which can differ.

On a sale, the local treasurer's guidance applies. The Muskingum County Treasurer states that the owner of record receives the bill and that taxes "should be prorated at closing," with the seller crediting the buyer for the prorated share on the closing statement. Other treasurers handle the same process similarly, but a title agent computes the figure.

The deed's statement of value also surfaces two items. If the home received a tax reduction under section 323.152, the statement must address it. If the land was in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program, a recoupment charge under section 5713.34 may apply when it stops qualifying.

What happens to the seller's mortgage payoff at closing?

The payoff is taken from your proceeds and paid to the lender. The lender then owes a duty under section 5301.36: record a release of the mortgage within ninety days of satisfaction. The statute lets the lender recover the recording fee from the borrower by contract.

If a release is not recorded, the owner can send a written notice, and the lender then has fifteen days before damages of $100 per day begin, capped at $5,000. A mortgagor may also recover $250 in damages for a late release. Check the county recorder's index after closing to confirm it posted.

What disclosures does an Ohio seller owe the buyer?

Anyone selling a home with up to four dwelling units must complete the state's property disclosure form and deliver a signed copy to the buyer, under section 5302.30. The form covers water supply, sewer, structure, hazardous materials and known defects.

A buyer who receives the form after signing the contract can rescind within three business days, and no later than the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. Exceptions include court-ordered transfers, estate fiduciary transfers, and a seller who inherited the home and has not lived there in the past year. If a buyer is borrowing, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains that the lender must provide a Closing Disclosure three business days before closing, and its seller-side lines cover credits and prorations.

What does an Ohio seller get back at closing?

A closing statement runs in two directions. Besides charges, a seller can be owed money, most often a refund of taxes or other items prepaid beyond the closing date. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's explainer describes how the buyer's Closing Disclosure shows costs the seller prepaid that the buyer reimburses, and prior taxes and fees the seller owes that the buyer will pay later and the seller covers now. Those lines are where tax prorations land.

The same explainer notes that a seller may agree to contribute to the buyer's closing costs, either as a general amount or as named "Seller Paid" items. If you offer a credit to win a sale, ask for the figure to appear on the contract and on the final statement so it matches.

The net you carry away is the sale price less the payoff, the statutory fees above, any agreed credits and the tax proration. Ask the title agent for a draft statement several days before closing so you can compare each line against the table on this page and the county's printed rate.

More questions about Ohio Closing Costs

What is the Ohio conveyance fee?

It is $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is greater, under Revised Code 319.54(G)(3). A county may add up to thirty cents per hundred more, and the seller pays both.

Does Ohio have a state transfer tax?

Ohio's charge is collected by the county auditor, not as a single flat state rate. The statutory fee has a floor, and counties may levy an optional tax with a ceiling of thirty cents per hundred dollars.

Who pays recording fees on an Ohio sale?

The statute sets the amount but does not assign it. The purchase contract decides, so check the settlement statement or ask the title agent which side carries the deed's recording fee.

How soon must a lender record a mortgage release in Ohio?

Within ninety days after the mortgage is satisfied. If it is late, the owner can give written notice, and the lender then has fifteen days to record before daily damages start.

Are inherited-house sales exempt from the Ohio disclosure form?

Sometimes. The property disclosure statute exempts a seller who got the property by inheritance and has not lived in it within the past year, as well as transfers by estate fiduciaries.
